editorialNote: Original educational analysis of public primary sources. Documented decisions and editorial inferences are distinguished. Interview and team work are not represented as sole-authored essays. No prototypes were executed or accessibility-audited.

people.name: Emmet Connolly
people.keyIdea: A principle is useful when it resolves a real tradeoff; an interface is useful when its modality matches the task.

artifacts.title: Introducing Intercom’s product principles
artifacts.author: Emmet Connolly
artifacts.summary: Explains how explicit principles preserve shared judgment as an organization grows, and why a principle should have a plausible opposite.

artifacts.title: Principles of bot design
artifacts.author: Emmet Connolly
artifacts.summary: A pre-LLM proposal for clear bot identity, bounded interactions, structured choices, and human escape routes. Its capability assumptions belong to 2016.

artifacts.title: Off Script: Designing the future with AI
artifacts.author: Emmet Connolly, speaking; introduction by Davin O’Dwyer
artifacts.sourceType: Official video and lightly edited transcript
artifacts.summary: Argues that AI can change product categories and interface forms. A billing-address example shows why a compact form can outperform a sequence of chat questions.

decisions.decision: Codify decision intent rather than make process the final authority.
decisions.alternative: Require an identical workflow for every project.
decisions.tradeoff: Principles allow adaptation but demand judgment; process is easier to audit and can protect novices. The tradeoff is editorial analysis of his argument.

decisions.decision: Test a proposed principle by writing its plausible opposite.
decisions.alternative: Adopt agreeable slogans that cannot resolve disagreement.
decisions.tradeoff: A sharp preference makes tradeoffs explicit but can be wrong in another company or phase.

decisions.decision: Give bots a clear identity and an escape route to a human.
decisions.alternative: Imitate human behavior or keep the user inside automation at all costs.
decisions.tradeoff: Transparency and recovery can reduce frustration, but human escalation requires operational capacity. His narrow-interaction advice is historical, not a current model limit.
decisions.status: Documented 2016 recommendations; contemporary application is analysis

decisions.decision: Use a structured form inside an AI interaction when fields are the efficient representation.
decisions.alternative: Ask for each address field in a separate chat turn.
decisions.tradeoff: A widget reduces turn-taking but requires a safe rendering system and may constrain unexpected input. These implementation consequences are analysis.
decisions.status: Documented 2024 scenario; not a reported controlled experiment

writingTechniques.technique: Turn an abstract claim into a falsifiable editing test.
writingTechniques.evidence: The product-principles essay contrasts empty agreement with a preference whose opposite is reasonable, so the reader can evaluate their own wording.
The bot essay names concrete behaviors and closes by admitting that future capabilities or experience may invalidate its rules.

writingTechniques.technique: Act out the slow version before showing the alternative.
writingTechniques.evidence: In the AI transcript, the billing-address conversation exposes turn-taking overhead before introducing a form. This is presentation technique, not evidence of sole-authored prose.

exercise.task: Choose a customer-service workflow. Write three principles with reasonable opposites, then build both a chat-only and a mixed form/chat version of its most tedious step.
exercise.deliverable: A two-prototype comparison, an escalation map, and a one-page principle document separating enduring user needs from capability-dependent assumptions.
evaluation: Can each principle choose between two credible alternatives?
Compare task completion, correction cost, and number of turns.
Show users what is automated and how to recover.
Identify which conclusions would change if model reliability improved.

limitations: The 2016 bot essay predates modern LLMs; its interaction constraints should not be presented as timeless.
These are first-party arguments and examples, not independent performance evaluations.
The 2024 piece is an edited spoken transcript with a separate introduction, not an essay written solely by Connolly.
people.coverage: Three primary artifacts read: two bylined essays and one official transcript. The contrast across 2016 and 2024 illustrates evolving interface choices without assuming an undocumented personal change of mind.

people.name: Raphael Salaja
people.keyIdea: The finishing pass is a system-level judgment: remove, align, and test repeated use rather than accept locally plausible details.

artifacts.title: What the Model Misses
artifacts.author: Raphael Salaja
artifacts.summary: Uses an AI-generated card to show how individually plausible choices can become inconsistent when assembled. The proposed finishing pass removes decoration, aligns tokens, and makes state copy specific.

artifacts.title: On Copying
artifacts.author: Raphael Salaja
artifacts.sourceType: Personal essay and interactive learning example
artifacts.summary: Recommends privately reconstructing a small interaction to discover its spacing, timing, and structure, while distinguishing learning from passing someone else’s work off as original.

artifacts.title: A Note on Timing
artifacts.author: Raphael Salaja
artifacts.sourceType: Personal essay with controlled motion comparisons
artifacts.summary: Separates duration from curve and distance, then relates timing to repetition, travel, and whether an element is entering or leaving.

artifacts.title: Cambio
artifacts.author: Raphael Salaja / Cambio project
artifacts.summary: Documents a dialog-based morphing component built on Base UI and Motion, with shared presets, local overrides, dismissal controls, and reduced-motion behavior.

decisions.decision: Delete unnecessary decoration before tuning the remaining system.
decisions.alternative: Keep every generated flourish and polish each independently.
decisions.tradeoff: Subtraction can improve coherence and repeated use, while excessive removal can erase helpful feedback or identity.
decisions.status: Documented personal editing process; tradeoff analysis

decisions.decision: Reconstruct one small interaction and vary one parameter at a time.
decisions.alternative: Copy an entire product or collect visual references without implementing them.
decisions.tradeoff: A narrow exercise reveals causal relationships but does not teach the original product’s broader constraints.

decisions.decision: Shorten motion as frequency rises, and consider faster exits than entrances.
decisions.alternative: Apply one default duration to all transitions.
decisions.tradeoff: Less waiting serves expert repetition; excessive speed can hide state relationships or impair perception. Test the actual task instead of treating his values as universal constants.

decisions.decision: Combine a shared motion preset with component-level overrides and reduced-motion handling.
decisions.tradeoff: Defaults promote consistency while overrides preserve context; too many exceptions can fragment the system. Composition on accessible primitives is a starting point, not a completed audit.

writingTechniques.technique: Compare the same object before and after a specific editing pass.
writingTechniques.evidence: The model-output essay makes subtraction and consistency visible in one card rather than relying on general claims about taste.

writingTechniques.technique: Separate variables so readers can perceive a difference.
writingTechniques.evidence: The timing essay holds the interaction comparable while changing duration, then asks readers to consider repeated use.

writingTechniques.technique: Turn observation into a reproducible practice with an ethical boundary.
writingTechniques.evidence: The copying essay proceeds from close observation to a small reconstruction and explicitly distinguishes study from uncredited publication.

exercise.task: Choose one generated component you own. Record five repetitions, remove nonessential decoration, align its spacing and motion, and rewrite vague state copy. Compare three durations while keeping the curve fixed.
exercise.deliverable: A before/after recording, a token table, and a decision log explaining every deletion and retained animation.
evaluation: Can another person identify the current state without explanation?
Does the fifth repetition still feel responsive?
Does interruption work, and is reduced motion usable?
Can every flourish justify its cost or intentional expressive purpose?

limitations: The motion examples and numeric values are heuristics, not universal performance or accessibility thresholds.
Cambio’s documented reduced-motion and primitive choices were read but not exercised with assistive technology.
The critique of generated output is an argued example, not a study of all models or prompts.
people.coverage: Three full personal essays and one project documentation site read. Analysis focuses on repeatable methods rather than attributing broad industry outcomes.

people.name: Samuel Kraft
people.keyIdea: Useful craft emerges when the data model, navigation state, and animation lifecycle agree.

artifacts.title: Styling Radix UI with CSS
artifacts.author: Samuel Kraft
artifacts.summary: Shows how behavior primitives and CSS styling can be combined, then extracts repeated wrapper code into a helper for a design-system API.

artifacts.title: Responsive Animations with Framer Motion
artifacts.author: Samuel Kraft
artifacts.summary: Compares JavaScript media-query hooks with CSS-variable-driven variants, including server-rendering considerations. Credits Sam Selikoff for the CSS-variable approach.

artifacts.title: Building a mapping platform with React and Mapbox GL
artifacts.author: Samuel Kraft
artifacts.summary: Documents Trail Routes from route-data choices through map layers, URL-driven selection, and an animated sidebar’s final hidden state.

decisions.decision: Separate accessible interaction behavior from visual styling, then abstract repeated wrappers.
decisions.alternative: Reimplement each primitive or duplicate styling glue.
decisions.tradeoff: Reuse reduces repeated behavior work; wrappers must preserve the library’s evolving component and ref contracts.
decisions.status: Documented implementation approach; current compatibility is unverified

decisions.decision: Choose between media-query hooks and CSS-variable animation values based on rendering constraints.
decisions.tradeoff: JavaScript offers explicit state; CSS can avoid waiting for client-side measurement in server-rendered interfaces. Neither replaces testing breakpoint changes during an animation.
decisions.status: Documented comparison; additional test recommendation is analysis

decisions.decision: Use curated GPX data after the Strava route feed proved hard to categorize.
decisions.alternative: Keep a live API as the primary content source.
decisions.tradeoff: Curation gives control and predictable metadata but creates maintenance work and can become stale.

decisions.decision: Derive selected map layers from URL state and explicitly finish the sidebar’s hidden state.
decisions.alternative: Update only in click handlers and leave an invisible sidebar in layout.
decisions.tradeoff: Navigation and visual state become consistent at the cost of more lifecycle handling.

writingTechniques.technique: Earn an abstraction by first showing the duplication it removes.
writingTechniques.evidence: The Radix tutorial progresses from direct styling to repeated wrappers before introducing a shared helper.

writingTechniques.technique: Compare solutions against a concrete environmental constraint.
writingTechniques.evidence: The responsive-motion tutorial makes server rendering a reason to choose an approach, rather than declaring one technique always superior.

writingTechniques.technique: Explain the rejected route and the observed bug.
writingTechniques.evidence: The map case study includes both the abandoned data source and the invisible sidebar’s layout problem, making the finished design less mysterious.

exercise.task: Build a small catalog with a selectable map or diagram. Make selection URL-addressable, adapt its motion across two breakpoints, and ensure hidden panels no longer affect layout.
exercise.deliverable: A runnable prototype plus a test matrix for direct links, reload, back/forward, resize, and interrupted transitions.
evaluation: Do direct navigation and clicking produce the same state?
Does server-rendered content avoid a distracting initial jump?
Are offscreen controls actually unfocusable or appropriately hidden?
Which data deserves curation, and who keeps it current?

limitations: The code dates from 2021–2023. Verify current React, Radix, Motion, and Mapbox APIs rather than copying snippets unchanged.
The published wrappers and snippets are teaching examples, not a current production-ready package.
The route-metadata discussion is not an accuracy study; elevation computation and preprocessing details require independent validation.
people.coverage: Three primary tutorials/case studies read. Historical code is treated as evidence of reasoning, not a recommendation of exact current implementation.

people.name: Katie Dill
people.keyIdea: Quality must survive the complete customer journey, not only the review presentation or the best-looking screen.

artifacts.title: Craft and beauty: The business value of form in function
artifacts.author: Katie Dill, with panelists Karri Saarinen and Yuhki Yamashita
artifacts.summary: Dill connects visual clarity, product structure, and end-to-end experience. Her email example combines changes in copy, hierarchy, and journey design; it does not isolate beauty as a causal variable.

artifacts.title: Inside How Stripe Crafts Quality Products
artifacts.author: Katie Dill, interviewed and published by Peter Yang
artifacts.summary: Describes friction logs, reviews of 15 essential journeys, and a mix of customer, operational, and qualitative quality measures.

artifacts.title: How Stripe Built Their New Website
artifacts.author: Katie Dill, interviewed by Aaron Epstein; Stripe team work
artifacts.sourceType: Original YC video interview; transcript retrieved from the linked YouTube video
artifacts.confidence: high for retrieved interview; not independently tested
artifacts.summary: Explains why a broader product portfolio required a clearer homepage story, and how overlays let visitors explore offerings without leaving the page.

decisions.decision: Assess the whole journey across product, email, discovery, and support.
decisions.tradeoff: Cross-surface review catches handoff failures but requires coordination beyond one team’s immediate ownership.

decisions.decision: Review the working experience and combine several quality signals instead of relying on a polished deck or single score.
decisions.alternative: Let the presenter’s explanation and one metric stand in for user experience.
decisions.tradeoff: Direct use removes some framing bias, while internal reviewers still need outside-user evidence.
decisions.status: Documented practices; caveat follows interview’s limits

decisions.decision: Use progressive disclosure through homepage overlays rather than immediately sending every visitor to a product page.
decisions.alternative: Expand the homepage indefinitely or route users away at their first exploratory click.
decisions.tradeoff: Preserves browsing context but adds modal complexity and creates additional accessibility/navigation obligations.
decisions.status: Documented team choice explained by Dill; tradeoff analysis

decisions.decision: Delay a self-directed homepage launch to improve a prominent animation sequence.
decisions.alternative: Ship the rough sequence, simplify it, or remove it.
decisions.tradeoff: Brand expression received extra time because the team judged the delay tolerable; this is not a rule to postpone user-critical releases.
decisions.status: Documented contextual decision, not general delivery advice

writingTechniques.technique: Connect an abstract quality claim to layers of a familiar physical object.
writingTechniques.evidence: The Sessions talk uses a house to connect underlying structure with visible finish. The metaphor teaches dependency rather than just decoration.

writingTechniques.technique: Translate a value into repeatable operating behavior.
writingTechniques.evidence: The written interview moves from quality as an ideal to recurring journey reviews and complementary evidence. Interview structure also reflects Peter Yang’s editing.

writingTechniques.technique: Explain the business change before showing the redesign.
writingTechniques.evidence: The YC discussion grounds the homepage decisions in a broader product offering, then walks through the resulting interface. This is spoken explanation of team work.

exercise.task: Walk one customer journey from discovery through completion and recovery without a presenter’s explanation. Include at least one surface owned by another team. Redesign the highest-impact handoff and compare two disclosure patterns.
exercise.deliverable: A friction log, a journey map, one prototype, and a small quality scorecard combining task success, user sentiment, and observed defects.
evaluation: Can a new user understand the next step without coaching?
Which issue crosses an ownership boundary?
Does the redesign improve a measured outcome rather than only a review impression?
State the opportunity cost and reason for any extra polish time.

limitations: Business lift figures are company-reported and combine multiple changes; they do not establish that aesthetics alone caused improvement.
Interviews and talks are not sole-authored essays, and Stripe’s product/site work belongs to a team.
No live homepage usability, performance, or accessibility test was conducted.
The video’s publication date is corroborated by its episode metadata; the Sessions page identifies 2024 without an exact day.
people.coverage: Three primary artifacts: an official talk transcript, an original written interview, and an original YC video with retrieved transcript. Analysis attributes only Dill’s explanations, not all panelists’ statements or sole credit for Stripe work.
